theme: When Israel went out of Egypt, the sea fled
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 114. It has only eight verses, and it is one of the most compressed poems in the Psalter. Read it twice, once as a celebration of the exodus and once as a call to tremble before God.
settingTheScene: This is the third psalm in a row that looks back at the exodus. Psalm 106 was a confession, Psalm 77 was a memory in distress, and Psalm 114 is a burst of joy. It is part of the “Egyptian Hallel,” Psalms 113 to 118, which Jewish families have sung at the Passover meal for centuries. It was probably among the songs that Jesus and his disciples sang after the Last Supper (Mark 14:26). In just a few lines, it tells the whole story of redemption through the language of nature responding to God.
observation: “When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language” (v. 1).
“Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion” (v. 2).
“The sea looked and fled; Jordan turned back” (v. 3).
“The mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs” (v. 4).
The psalmist asks the sea, the Jordan, and the mountains what is wrong with them (vv. 5-6).
“Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob” (v. 7).
“Who turns the rock into a pool of water, the flint into a spring of water” (v. 8).
The psalm has two halves: verses 1 to 4 describe what happened, and verses 5 to 8 call the earth to respond.
interpretation:
The psalm does something unusual. It tells the story of the exodus without ever naming God until verse 7. The whole description is of Israel and the world’s reaction. The sea flees. The river turns back. The mountains leap. The poet leaves God offstage in order to make you feel his presence, like seeing the effect of a hurricane without the storm.

Verse 2 contains the heart of the exodus: “Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion.” God did not just free Israel. He claimed them. They were redeemed to be his dwelling place and his kingdom. This is the purpose of the exodus: not just freedom from but freedom for. It is the same as the promise in Exodus 6:7: “I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God.”

The questions of verses 5 and 6 are a bit of poetic humor. The poet asks the sea, “What is wrong with you?” The answer is not stated, but it is obvious: the Lord is here. Creation is not a neutral stage. It is a servant of God, and when he moves, it responds. The sea and the river, which seemed so powerful to ancient people, flee at his command.

The last verse is the most wonderful. After the earth trembles, the God who made it “turns the rock into a pool of water.” He is not only the one who shakes mountains. He is also the one who turns hard stone into fresh water for thirsty people. The God of power is also the God of provision, and you will see this very story in tomorrow’s reading at Massah and Meribah. The same hand does both.

The progression of the psalm is worth noticing. It begins with a historic event. It moves to the response of nature. And it ends with a command to the whole earth to tremble before the presence of the Lord. This is what the exodus is meant to do. It is not just a story about the past. It is a call to every creature to recognize who God is.
connection: Paul writes that Christ is “the rock” that followed Israel (1 Corinthians 10:4). Jesus said that he is the source of “living water” (John 4:14; 7:37-38). At Jesus’ death, the earth shook and the rocks were split (Matthew 27:51), and creation responded again to its Lord. Isaiah 44:3 and 48:21 also describe God providing water from the rock.
application:
Spend a few minutes outside this week, and notice the creation around you as a servant of God. Thank him for the rain, the rivers, and the hills.

Ask yourself if you tremble before the Lord, or if you have grown casual. Ask him to restore a healthy sense of awe.

Thank Jesus for being the rock from which living water flows.
prayerPrompts: Tremble and rejoice before God, as the earth does.
Thank him for Jesus, who gives living water.
Tell him what you want to bring out of “Egypt” in your own life.
